title: Sum-Free Set
content: A set $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is sum-free if $\forall a, b \in S,\; a + b \notin S$. Equivalently, $(S + S) \cap S = \emptyset$ where $S + S = \{a + b : a, b \in S\}$. Note this allows $a = b$, so $2a \notin S$ for any $a \in S$. Sum-free subsets of $\{1, \ldots, n\}$ have been extensively studied: the maximum size is $\lceil n/2 \rceil$ (achieved by the odd numbers in $[n/2, n]$). In $\mathbb{R}$, the structure is richer due to the continuum cardinality.
mathContext: $\text{IsSumFreeSet}(S) \iff \forall a \in S,\; \forall b \in S,\; a + b \notin S \iff (S + S) \cap S = \emptyset$

title: Sidon Set in ℝ
content: A set $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is Sidon if all pairwise sums $a + b$ with $a \leq b$ are distinct: $a + b = c + d$ with $a \leq b, c \leq d$ implies $(a, b) = (c, d)$. In finite sets, Sidon sets have size $O(\sqrt{n})$ in $\{1, \ldots, n\}$. In $\mathbb{R}$, Sidon sets can be uncountable (e.g., algebraically independent sets over $\mathbb{Q}$). Sidon sets are NOT necessarily sum-free—the file proves this with the counterexample $\{1, 2, 4\}$.
mathContext: $\text{IsSidonReal}(S) \iff \forall a \leq b,\; c \leq d \in S:\; a + b = c + d \implies (a,b) = (c,d)$

title: The Sumset A + A
content: The sumset $A + A = \{a + b : a, b \in A\}$ collects all pairwise sums from $A$. This is the image of the addition map $A \times A \to \mathbb{R}$. If $|A| = \aleph_0$, then $|A+A| \leq \aleph_0$. If $|A| = \mathfrak{c}$, then $|A+A| \leq \mathfrak{c}$. The problem asks for $A$ with $(A+A) \cap S = \emptyset$, i.e., the sumset avoids the original sum-free set entirely.
mathContext: $\text{realSumset}(A) = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : \exists a \in A,\; \exists b \in A,\; x = a + b\} = A + A$

title: Erdős Problem 949: Main Conjecture
content: For every sum-free $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, there exists $A \subseteq S^c$ with $|A| = \mathfrak{c}$ (the cardinality of the continuum) and $A + A \subseteq S^c$. This asks: does a sum-free set always leave enough additive room in its complement for a continuum-sized set whose sumset also stays in the complement? The continuum cardinality is essential—the question is trivial for countable $A$ since $S^c$ always has cardinality $\mathfrak{c}$ (as $S$ is sum-free, hence cannot be all of $\mathbb{R}$).
mathContext: $\forall S \subseteq \mathbb{R},\; \text{IsSumFreeSet}(S) \implies \exists A \subseteq S^c:\; |A| = \mathfrak{c} \wedge A + A \subseteq S^c$

title: Odd Numbers Are Sum-Free (Proved)
content: The set of odd positive reals $\{2n+1 : n \in \mathbb{N}\}$ is sum-free because odd + odd = even, so the sum never lands in the set. The proof uses `ring` to show $2m + 1 + 2n + 1 = 2(m+n+1)$ (even), then derives a contradiction if this equals $2k + 1$ (odd) via `omega`. This is the simplest concrete example of a sum-free set in the formalization.

title: Sidon Does Not Imply Sum-Free (Proved)
content: The theorem `sidon_not_implies_sum_free` proves that $\{1, 2, 4\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is Sidon (all 6 pairwise sums $2, 3, 5, 3, 5, 8$ with repetitions but distinct ordered sums) yet not sum-free since $1 + 1 = 2 \in S$. This corrects a previous unsound axiom `sidon_is_sum_free`. The proof constructs the Sidon verification by case analysis on all element combinations (12 cases) and shows the sum-free property fails by exhibiting the witness $a = b = 1$.
mathContext: $\{1, 2, 4\}$ is Sidon (B₂) but $1 + 1 = 2 \in S$, so Sidon $\not\Rightarrow$ sum-free

title: Sidon Variant (Solved by Dillies-AlphaProof)
content: The Sidon variant of Problem 949 is proved: if $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is Sidon, then there exists $A \subseteq S^c$ with $|A| = \mathfrak{c}$ and $A + A \subseteq S^c$. Note this does NOT require $S$ to be sum-free. The proof splits into two cases: (1) if $|S| < \mathfrak{c}$, Zorn's lemma produces a maximal sumset-avoiding subset of $S^c$, and maximality forces $|A| = \mathfrak{c}$; (2) if $|S| = \mathfrak{c}$, pick $a \neq 0$ in $S$ and form $A = ((S \setminus \{a\}) - a/2) \setminus S$, where the Sidon property ensures the image has at most one element in $S$.
mathContext: $\forall S \subseteq \mathbb{R},\; \text{IsSidonReal}(S) \implies \exists A \subseteq S^c:\; |A| = \mathfrak{c} \wedge A + A \subseteq S^c$

title: General Sum-Free Case Remains Open
content: The general Problem 949 for arbitrary sum-free sets remains open. The key difficulty: sum-free sets can be much denser than Sidon sets (sum-free subsets of $[n]$ can have $\sim n/2$ elements, while Sidon subsets have $\sim \sqrt{n}$). The Sidon proof exploits the injectivity of the sum map ($a + b = c + d \implies (a,b) = (c,d)$), which fails for general sum-free sets. The axiom `erdos_949_open` records the full conjecture.
mathContext: ErdosProblem949 is stated as an axiom: the general case $\text{IsSumFreeSet}(S) \implies \exists A$ with the required properties is OPEN
relatedConcepts: density gap between Sidon and sum-free
